title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: Is it true that for every 2-edge-connected graph $G$, the reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,5)$ is connected?
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops. Given an abelian group $A$, an $A$-flow of $G$ is an orientation of the edges together with values $f:E(G)\to A$ such that at every vertex the sum of incoming values equals the sum of outgoing values; for an integer $k\ge 2$, a $k$-flow is a $\mathbb{Z}$-flow whose values are all less than $k$ in absolute value; a flow is nowhere-zero if no edge gets value $0$. The reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ (resp. $\mathcal{F}(G,A)$) has the nowhere-zero $k$-flows (resp. $A$-flows) of $G$ as vertices, two flows being adjacent if and only if the support of their difference is a cycle (a connected 2-regular subgraph), i.e. one is obtained from the other by adding some value along a cycle; the empty graph counts as connected. This is the natural reconfiguration version of Tutte's 5-flow conjecture; it is incomparable with it, since connectedness of $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ does not imply non-emptiness. The group-flow analogue (with $\mathbb{Z}_5$) is posed separately. Note that the same paper answers this problem negatively: it constructs a graph $G$ with a nowhere-zero $\mathbb{Z}_5$-flow that is an isolated vertex of $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_5)$, so that both $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_5)$ and $\mathcal{F}(G,5)$ are disconnected (the abstract states that the reconfiguration variant of Tutte's 5-flow conjecture is false in the group and integer cases). The weaker question whether some integer $k\ge5$ makes $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ connected for every 2-edge-connected $G$ is also raised.

title: Problem 1.2
statement_text: Is there an integer $k\geqslant 5$, such that for every 2-edge-connected graph $G$, the reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ is connected?
context_text: This is a weaker variant of Problem 1.1: rather than asking whether $k=5$ suffices, it asks whether any fixed integer $k$ makes the integer-flow reconfiguration graph universally connected. It is posed immediately after Problem 1.1 as a relaxation of interest.

title: Problem 1.3
statement_text: Is it true that for every 2-edge-connected graph $G$, the reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_{5})$ is connected?
context_text: This is the group-flow analogue of Problem 1.1, asking about $\mathbb{Z}_5$-flows instead of integer 5-flows. The paper shows that connectivity of the flow reconfiguration graph depends on the group structure, making the group and integer settings genuinely distinct.

title: Problem 1.4
statement_text: Is there an abelian group $A$, such that for every 2-edge-connected graph $G$, the reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,A)$ is connected?
context_text: This asks for the existence of any abelian group making the group-flow reconfiguration graph universally connected. The paper shows that frozen configurations (isolated vertices) do not exist in $\mathcal{F}(G,A)$ whenever $|A|=4$ or $|A|\geqslant 6$, but that $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_5)$ can contain frozen flows, complicating the picture.

title: Problem 2.6
statement_text: Let $G$ be a graph and $k$ be an integer. Prove that if $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_{k})$ is connected, then $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ is also connected.
context_text: Graphs may have multiple edges but no loops. Given an abelian group $A$, an $A$-flow of $G$ is an orientation of the edges together with values $f:E(G)\to A$ such that at every vertex the sum of incoming values equals the sum of outgoing values; for an integer $k\ge 2$, a $k$-flow is a $\mathbb{Z}$-flow whose values are all less than $k$ in absolute value; a flow is nowhere-zero if no edge gets value $0$. The reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ (resp. $\mathcal{F}(G,A)$) has the nowhere-zero $k$-flows (resp. $A$-flows) of $G$ as vertices, two flows being adjacent if and only if the support of their difference is a cycle (a connected 2-regular subgraph); the empty graph counts as connected. $\mathbb{Z}_k$ is the cyclic group of order $k$. The paper observes the easy direction: if $\mathcal{F}(G,k)$ is connected then $\mathcal{F}(G,\mathbb{Z}_k)$ is connected. Unlike for the existence of nowhere-zero flows (which by Tutte depends only on $|A|$), the group structure matters for reconfiguration: $\mathcal{F}(K_4,\mathbb{Z}_4)$ is disconnected while $\mathcal{F}(K_4,\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2)$ is connected. The authors believe the converse of the observation holds, but cannot prove it even for $k=4$.
